adorno: Theodor Adorno (1903–1969) was a German philosopher and sociologist of the Frankfurt School, blending Marxist critique with aesthetics. With Max Horkheimer he coined the 'culture industry' critique, arguing that mass-produced entertainment standardizes thought and quietly pacifies its audiences.
aquinas: Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274) was an Italian Dominican friar and the towering philosopher-theologian of the Middle Ages, synthesizing Aristotle with Christian doctrine. Known for the Five Ways (arguments for God's existence), natural law theory, and the doctrine of double effect, his Summa Theologiae remains foundational to Catholic philosophy.
arendt: Hannah Arendt (1906–1975) was a German-American political philosopher who fled Nazi Germany, writing on the origins of totalitarianism and the fragility of public freedom. She coined 'the banality of evil' while covering the trial of Adolf Eichmann: monstrous wrong done by ordinary, thoughtless functionaries.
baudrillard: Jean Baudrillard (1929–2007) was a French social theorist and a leading, often deliberately provocative, voice of postmodernism. His central idea, 'simulacra and simulation,' holds that in media-saturated societies images and copies replace reality, producing the 'hyperreal' — a point The Matrix helped make famous.
boethius: Boethius (c. 477–524) was a Roman statesman and Christian philosopher, executed on treason charges while awaiting death. His prison-written Consolation of Philosophy — a dialogue on fortune, evil, free will, and God's foreknowledge — became one of the most-read books of the Middle Ages.
buddha: The Buddha (Siddhartha Gautama, traditionally c. 563–483 BC) taught the Four Noble Truths: life involves suffering rooted in craving, and liberation from it is achievable through the Eightfold Path. His doctrines of impermanence and non-self — the rejection of any permanent soul — anchor centuries of Buddhist philosophy.
camus: Albert Camus (1913–1960) was a French-Algerian novelist, essayist, and Nobel laureate who rejected the existentialist label often pinned on him. His philosophy of the Absurd — the clash between our craving for meaning and the universe's silence — drives The Myth of Sisyphus, where he answers despair with lucid, nonviolent revolt.
dennett: Daniel Dennett (1942–2024) was an American philosopher of mind and a leading naturalist, known for the 'intentional stance' (treating minds as belief-and-desire systems) and for arguing that free will is compatible with determinism. He insisted consciousness needs no mysterious extra ingredient, contending with Chalmers' 'hard problem.'
dostoevsky: Fyodor Dostoevsky was a nineteenth-century Russian novelist whose fiction is read as philosophy: Notes from Underground, Crime and Punishment, and The Brothers Karamazov probe free will, faith and doubt, and the psychology of rebellion. He is widely regarded as a crucial precursor of existentialism.
epicurus: Epicurus (341–270 BC) founded an Athenian school, the Garden, teaching that pleasure is the highest good — understood as tranquil peace of mind (ataraxia), not indulgence. Building on Democritus' atomism, he argued that death 'is nothing to us,' since the soul dissolves when the body does.
feyerabend: Paul Feyerabend (1924–1994) was an Austrian-born philosopher of science, trained under Popper, who turned against every fixed theory of method. In Against Method he defended 'epistemological anarchism,' provocatively summed up as 'anything goes': no single rule captures how science actually advances.
gandhi: Mahatma Gandhi (1869–1948) was an Indian lawyer and independence leader whose philosophy of satyagraha made nonviolence (ahimsa) a disciplined political method, not merely a private virtue. Drawing on Hindu ideas of truth and self-suffering alongside Tolstoy and Thoreau, he reworked how the modern world thinks about resistance.
habermas: Jürgen Habermas (b. 1929) is Germany's most prominent living philosopher and a second-generation member of the Frankfurt School. Best known for his account of the 'public sphere' and communicative rationality, he argues democracy works through inclusive, reasoned public debate rather than market forces or state power.
hegel: G.W.F. Hegel (1770–1831) was the great German idealist, arguably the most systematic philosopher of the modern era. His dialectic — development through contradiction — and his account of Geist (spirit) realizing freedom through history shaped Marx, while the master–slave dialectic inspired later politics of recognition.
horkheimer: Max Horkheimer was a German philosopher and longtime director of the Frankfurt School's Institute for Social Research, who named its program 'critical theory.' With Adorno he co-wrote Dialectic of Enlightenment, whose 'culture industry' chapter argues that mass media manufactures conformity.
hume: David Hume (1711–1776) was a Scottish empiricist and skeptic, a central figure of the Enlightenment. He argued that all ideas derive from experience, that causation is habit rather than perception, that reason is 'the slave of the passions,' and that the self is just a bundle of impressions — puzzles still debated today.
jackson: Frank Jackson (b. 1943) is an Australian philosopher best known for the knowledge argument, or 'Mary's Room': a scientist who knows every physical fact about color, but has never seen it, seems to learn something new on her first glimpse of red. The thought experiment long stood as a major challenge to physicalism.
locke: John Locke (1632–1704) was an English empiricist and political philosopher often called the father of liberalism. He argued the mind begins as a blank slate, that personal identity consists in memory and consciousness, and that people have natural rights to life, liberty, and property — ideas that fed democratic revolutions.
plantinga: Alvin Plantinga (b. 1932) is an American analytic philosopher, widely considered the most influential contemporary philosopher of religion. Known for his 'free will defense' against the problem of evil, he also argues that belief in God can be rational without evidence or arguments — a view called Reformed epistemology.
popper: Karl Popper (1902–1994) was an Austrian-British philosopher of science who made falsifiability the dividing line between science and non-science: theories can never be conclusively verified, only tested and refuted. A fierce anti-totalitarian, he also defended liberal 'open societies' in The Open Society and Its Enemies.
richard-taylor: Richard Taylor was an American philosopher known for lucid work in metaphysics on free will, fate, and the meaning of life. Writing accessibly in books like Good and Evil, he argued that meaning is not an objective fact to discover but something found in wholehearted engagement with one's projects.
rousseau: Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712–1778) was a Genevan-born Enlightenment political philosopher who argued that humans are naturally good but corrupted by society. In The Social Contract he made the 'general will' the basis of legitimate government, ideas that profoundly influenced the French Revolution.
searle: John Searle (b. 1932) is an American philosopher at Berkeley, famous for the Chinese Room argument: that manipulating symbols by a program, however fluently, is not genuine understanding — a standing challenge to strong claims about AI. His 'biological naturalism' treats consciousness as a real biological effect of the brain.
william-james: William James (1842–1910) was an American psychologist and philosopher, a founder of pragmatism alongside Peirce and Dewey. He held that truth shows itself in practical consequences — 'truth is what works' — and, in 'The Will to Believe,' that in some forced, momentous choices we are entitled to faith without conclusive evidence.
